item.title: EpiPack: A computational framework for reference mapping and out-of-reference detection for single-cell ATAC-seq data with heterogeneous peak features
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78924-9

EpiPack maps single-cell chromatin accessibility data across heterogeneous datasets and identifies cell types and states absent from reference atlases, enabling analysis of disease-associated cellular changes.

item.title: Constructing radiative dipolar excitons via frontier-state hybridization in 2D perovskites
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79153-w

Dipolar excitons offer long-range interactions but typically suffer from weak optical activity. Yan et al. engineer frontier-state hybridization in a two-dimensional perovskite to realize optically active dipolar excitons with long-range repulsive interactions.

item.title: 4D mitochondrial network assumes distinct and predictive phenotypes through human lung and intestinal epithelial development
item.description:
Gillian McMahon, Dhruv Agarwal, Mehul Arora, Zichen Wang, Eric Arkfeld, Hiroyuki Hakozaki, Johannes Schöneberg
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78762-9
Abstract Mitochondria form dynamic three-dimensional networks that exhibit a wide range of morphology and motility depending on cell state, cell type, and cell fate. Isolated phenotypes have been described for individual cell states, but how mitochondrial morphology and motility change across the full course of human tissue development has so far been unclear. Human stem cell-derived branching lung and intestinal organoids mimic developing human organs and make these systems accessible. Here we show, by imaging at key developmental time points from human stem cell through mature organoid tissue with lattice light-sheet microscopy, that mitochondrial networks adopt morphology and motility signatures that vary with developmental stage, that mitochondrial and cellular features can be used to predict developmental stage, and that two-dimensional measurements obscure features resolved only in three dimensions over time, yielding an integrated map of mitochondrial phenotypes across human tissue development.
